formation.title: The City of Peace
formation.text:
The bridge of boats is remade across the Tigris and the khutba is read in a new name. Iraq has a government again.

What it does not have is the thing that made it rich. The Sawad was the highest-yielding tax province in the Islamic world for three hundred years because the canals worked. In 937, in a squalid war between two Turkish commanders, the Nahrawan was cut. Nobody with the money to repair it ever held the ground long enough to try. Tax receipts had already fallen by half before the Mongols arrived; Hulagu inherited a corpse and was blamed for the murder.

So the new state must decide what Baghdad is for. Al-Mansur called this place Madinat al-Salam, the City of Peace, and for two centuries it was two cities at once: the seat of the Commander of the Faithful, and the place where a Nestorian physician, a Sabian astronomer and a Persian grammarian argued in the same room and were all paid by the treasury. Those two Baghdads did not fall together, and they cannot both be rebuilt first.

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: Dar al-Khilafa: Baghdad rules Islam again

modifiers.name: Dar al-Khilafa
modifiers.text: The House of the Caliphate. Baghdad claims again the right to arbitrate between Muslim rulers, and the Shia of the shrine cities hear the claim exactly as it is meant.

effects.name: War Score vs other Religion Efficiency

options.text: Madinat al-Salam: Baghdad teaches it again

modifiers.name: Madinat al-Salam
modifiers.text: The City of Peace, under the name al-Mansur gave it. Translators, physicians and stationers are paid before soldiers are, and the barracks are the first thing to empty.

advances.name: The Survey of the Sawad
advances.text: The measured cadastre Anushirwan imposed on Mesopotamia, inherited whole by the Arab conquest and run from the diwan al-kharaj: every jarib of irrigated ground on a roll, and the tax fixed on the measurement.

advances.name: The Breach at Nahrawan
advances.text: The canal that carried Tigris water two hundred kilometres to feed the capital, cut in 937 during a war between two Turkish commanders and never properly repaired. Restoring the head regulators is this country's founding act.

event.title: The Breach at Nahrawan
event.text:
The engineers have walked the line from the Tigris offtake down past Baqubah to the old Wasit tail, and their report is not encouraging. Two hundred kilometres of channel, silted to the crown in places, the regulators robbed for their masonry, whole villages resettled onto the bed because the bed is the only ground that still holds moisture.

It can be dug. It has been dug before. The question the diwan cannot answer is who pays, and Iraq has only ever had two answers. The Abbasids in their strength mustered the villages by corvee and had the channel open in a season. The Abbasids in their weakness sold the works to the men who owned the land beside them, and never got the water back.

options.text: Muster the villages. The state digs its own canal.

modifiers.name: Corvee of the Sawad
modifiers.text: The villages are mustered with basket and rope and the channel is open in a season. The Sawad remembers being mustered.

options.text: Farm the works to the landholders for a share of the crop.

modifiers.name: Farmed Waterworks
modifiers.text: The landholders dredge their own canal for a standing share of the crop. It stays dredged, and the crown never again decides alone where the water goes.

advances.name: Palm Husbandry
advances.text: The date palm is propagated from offshoots rather than seed and planted in the three-tier garden, citrus below the palms and vegetables below the citrus. It fruits on saline ground in arid air, which no orchard tree will do.

advances.name: The Bataih
advances.text: The marsh belt between Kufa, Wasit and Basra, where the Zanj held out for fourteen years from a capital no cavalry army could reach. Whoever knows the causeways owns the ground.

advances.name: Halls of Reed
advances.text: The mudhif is a hall of bundled reeds raised on an island of mats and mud, rebuilt every generation. It is a fortification as much as a guest house, and an army that wants one has to wade to it.

advances.name: Scribes of the Diwan
advances.text: The secretarial class that actually ran the caliphate. Ibn Muqla fixed the proportions of the Arabic script so a document written in Basra read as authoritative in Baghdad; here bureaucracy is a literary profession with a house style.

advances.name: The Mustansiriya
advances.text: Al-Mustansir's school, opened in 1234, the first anywhere to teach all four schools of Sunni law under one roof with a library, a hospital and a pharmacy attached. It survived 1258 and it is still standing.

event.title: The Four Doors
event.text:
Al-Mustansir's school opened in 1234 with something no school had attempted: four iwans off one courtyard, one for each of the Sunni schools of law, so that a Hanafi and a Hanbali would cross the same paving on their way to teach. A library, a hospital and a pharmacy stood behind them. The Mongols burned much and this survived; it is still standing on the left bank.

The teaching posts are vacant and the endowment is in the crown's gift. Whoever is invited through those doors will define what Iraqi learning means for the next three centuries.

options.text: Cut a fifth door. Bring the jurists of Hilla in.

modifiers.name: The Fifth Door
modifiers.text: The Imami jurists of Hilla teach in the Mustansiriya courtyard beside the four Sunni schools. No other madrasa on earth seats them all.

options.text: Make it the judicial academy of the realm.

modifiers.name: School of the Qadis
modifiers.text: Every judge in the realm holds a licence signed in one courtyard, and that courtyard decides what the law is.

advances.name: The Stationers' Quarter
advances.text: Harun al-Rashid's papermakers worked linen and hemp rag because that is what Iraq had. The market that grew around them held over a hundred shops, and al-Jahiz rented one by the day to read the stock.

advances.name: The Thresholds
advances.text: Najaf, Karbala, Kazimayn and Samarra: four shrine cities inside the country's core, drawing pilgrims, endowments and corpses from Iran and India. A state here either comes to terms with them or fights them forever.

event.title: The Thresholds
event.text:
They are called the Atabat, the thresholds: Ali at Najaf on the desert edge, Husayn at Karbala, the two imams at Kazimayn across the water from Baghdad, the Askari shrine at Samarra. Four holy cities inside a hundred miles of the capital, each with its keeper families, its endowments and its own quiet diplomacy.

They are not only devotional. Money arrives from Awadh in India and from Isfahan. Corpses arrive by the caravan-load for burial in the Valley of Peace, and the men who carry them carry news. A ruler in Baghdad who ignores the shrine cities is ignoring the wealthiest and best-connected institution in his own country.

options.text: Endow them, appoint their keepers, take the offerings.

modifiers.name: Patron of the Thresholds
modifiers.text: The crown endows the shrines, appoints their keepers and banks the offerings. The keeper families do not forgive being appointed.

options.text: Leave them their own government. Take the pilgrim roads.

modifiers.name: Road of the Pilgrims
modifiers.text: The shrine cities keep their own government. The state escorts the caravans from Iran and India and takes the tolls, which pay better than the offerings would have.

advances.name: The Ayyarun
advances.text: The armed young men of Baghdad's quarters, half brotherhood and half gang, bound by futuwwa oath. They ran the city when the caliph could not and manned the walls in siege after siege.

advances.name: The Baghdad Atelier
advances.text: Sultan Ahmad Jalayir kept a painting workshop at Baghdad and wrote verse for it to illustrate. In the manuscripts made there around 1400 the Persianate miniature stops being decoration and becomes a picture.

advances.name: The Ubulla Roadstead
advances.text: The quay at the head of the Gulf, which the geographers called one of the four earthly paradises. Everything from India transships there, because a sea-going hull cannot take the shoals upstream.

advances.name: The Ghurab Squadron
advances.text: The raven: an oared gun-vessel shallow enough for the Shatt al-Arab bar and armed enough to argue with a carrack in confined water. Basra fought for the river mouth with these for two centuries.

event.title: The Mouth of the Gulf
event.text:
Everything that reaches Baghdad from India stops first at the head of the Gulf, because a hull built for the open sea cannot take the shoals of the lower rivers and a river boat cannot take the Gulf. The transhipment happens at Basra whether anyone plans it or not.

What has changed is that a European power now sits at the strait and charges for the passage. The yards can build ghurab, oared and heavily gunned and shallow enough for the bar, which will beat anything afloat in confined water and lose badly outside it. Or the port can be thrown open to every flag on the understanding that a customs house makes more money than a squadron.

options.text: Hold the bar. Nobody passes without our leave.

modifiers.name: Squadron at the Bar
modifiers.text: Oared gunboats hold the Shatt al-Arab where it meets salt water. Nothing passes without leave, and the quarrel over that never quite ends.

options.text: Open the roadstead. Every flag lands and every flag pays.

modifiers.name: The Open Roadstead
modifiers.text: Basra takes every flag and protects every hull upriver. The customs house earns more than a fleet would, and the neighbours call it weakness.

advances.name: The Muntafiq Emirate
advances.text: A confederation of the lower Euphrates, part settled cultivator and part camel nomad, that outlasted every governor sent against it and held the road between Basra and the desert.

advances.name: The Walls of Baghdad
advances.text: The city changed hands by siege in 1508, 1534, 1623 and 1638, and Murad IV's last assault cost him a third of his army. A city besieged every other generation keeps its cisterns full before anything else.

advances.name: Muqasama
advances.text: Al-Mahdi replaced the fixed area tax with a share of the actual crop: half on flood-irrigated ground, a third under a waterwheel, a quarter under an animal wheel. The treasury now loses when a canal silts, which is the only arrangement that makes it dredge.

advances.name: Afrasiyab Basra
advances.text: For seventy years Basra was run by a family who answered Istanbul only when it suited them, and kept the port open to Portuguese, Dutch and English factors, Persian pilgrims and Armenian brokers alike.

advances.name: Attabi Weaving
advances.text: A watered stripe of silk laid on cotton, named for the Baghdad quarter that wove it, and carried far enough that the word reached English as tabby. It is the one luxury textile a cotton country with almost no silk can make.

advances.name: The Desert Crossing
advances.text: The road from Baghdad to Aleppo runs straight across the Syrian desert instead of following the rivers north, and saves six weeks to anyone who dares it. By the 1780s London's letters to Bombay went this way.

advances.name: The Shrine Endowments
advances.text: Who appoints the keeper, who counts the offerings, whose pilgrims are admitted. The endowments were fought over in the archives as hard as any border, and the money behind them came from Awadh and Isfahan.

advances.name: The Bitumen of Hit
advances.text: Seeps worked since Babylon and described by Herodotus. The pitch caulked every craft on the Euphrates and every boom built at Basra, which is how a country with no pine forest keeps a fleet watertight.

advances.name: The Household
advances.text: Hasan Pasha bought Georgian boys, converted and schooled them and married them into each other's families. Within a generation the kuls were choosing the governor of Baghdad.

event.title: The Household
event.text:
Hasan Pasha came out from Istanbul as governor and started buying Georgian boys. He had them converted, schooled, taught horsemanship and accounts, and married into each other's families. Within a generation his kuls were the only competent administration between Mosul and the Gulf, and within two they were choosing the governor.

This is the oldest arrangement in the region and it has never once ended the way the buyer intended. The household is loyal, disciplined and effective. It is also, increasingly, the state, and it has no bloodline anyone can swear to.

options.text: Let the household govern. It governs well.

modifiers.name: Rule of the Kuls
modifiers.text: The bought household holds the divan, the treasury and the succession. It governs Iraq better than Istanbul managed, and it cannot produce a dynasty.

options.text: Seat the tribal shaykhs beside it and balance the two.

modifiers.name: Divan of Shaykhs
modifiers.text: The Muntafiq, the Khaza'il and the Zubayd sit at court beside the household. Between them they can raise every rider in Iraq and agree on nothing quickly.

advances.name: The Hindiyya Channel
advances.text: Money sent from Awadh cut a canal to Najaf in the 1790s. It worked so well that the Euphrates changed course, the desert between the shrine cities turned to farmland and rice fields, and the old Hilla branch began to die.

event.title: The Indian Canal
event.text:
Five hundred thousand rupees arrived from Awadh, sent by ministers who would never see Iraq, to cut a channel from the Euphrates to Najaf so the shrine city would have water. It worked better than anyone wanted. The river found the new bed agreeable and began to prefer it. Desert between Najaf and Karbala came under the plough within a decade and Sunni tribes moved in to farm it.

Downstream on the old Hilla branch the water is dropping. The gardens there are Abbasid-old. Holding both channels means building a masonry regulator at the fork, a work on a scale nobody in Iraq has attempted since the caliphs, and paying for it in silver the treasury does not have.

options.text: Let the Hindiyya run. Najaf blooms and Hilla is lost.

modifiers.name: Waters to Najaf
modifiers.text: The Euphrates takes the new bed. Desert between the shrine cities comes under the plough, and the old Hilla branch is left to the silt.

options.text: Build the regulator at the fork and hold both branches.

modifiers.name: Regulator at the Fork
modifiers.text: A masonry sluice holds both branches of the Euphrates open, the largest hydraulic work in Iraq since the caliphs, and it is paid for in coin the treasury had to mint.

advances.name: The Mamluk Pashalik
advances.text: The pashas of Baghdad governed as a dynasty in everything but name: they collected the tribute, appointed the judges, and fought Persia on their own account without asking whether they might.

advances.name: The Basra Customs
advances.text: The richest single revenue farm in Iraq, and whoever held it could pay for an army. Everything moving between the Gulf and Baghdad had to be weighed on that quay.

advances.name: The Hawza of Najaf
advances.text: The teaching circles settled at Najaf and the senior jurist there came to be followed from Lucknow to Jabal Amil. A seminary with no state behind it became the widest authority in Islam after the sultanate itself.

advances.name: The Land Code
advances.text: Title deeds were offered to tribesmen for ground their clans had farmed in common for centuries. The shaykhs registered it in their own names, and the reform meant to create smallholders created landlords.

advances.name: Al-Zawra
advances.text: A press arrives at the government house in 1869 and prints the first newspaper in Iraq. The copyists of the stationers' market had been reproducing books one at a time for a thousand years.

advances.name: The River Steamers
advances.text: Paddle steamers on the Tigris turn a month of raft and towpath into four days. Grain that could never previously reach a port suddenly can, and the whole geography of the country rearranges itself around the two rivers again.

advances.name: Conscription of the Tribes
advances.text: The draft reaches Iraq and the tribes answer with twenty years of rebellion. A state that wants soldiers from the Muntafiq and the Shammar has to garrison the ground it recruits from, and in the end it gets the men.

advances.name: The Saniyya Domain
advances.text: The crown takes the best land for itself: reclaimed marsh, canal frontage, the palm belt of the Shatt al-Arab, administered directly and paying no provincial tax. A private empire inside the public one.

destiny.name: The Register of Waters
destiny.text: A standing roll of every offtake, weir and sluice in the country: the canal, the villages that drink from it, the year it was last dredged, the silt at its mouth measured against a marked pole. Iraq has been dug out on emergency for six hundred years by men who never wrote down what they found.

conditions.text: Stability at least 25

event.title: The Register of Waters
event.text:
The inspectors have finished the first sweep. Every offtake from Samarra down to the head of the Gulf is on a roll now: the name of the channel, the villages that drink from it, the year it was last cleared, the depth of silt at its mouth measured against a marked pole. Four hundred and some entries, and a third of them describe works that no longer carry water at all.

Nobody has held this list before. The caliphs dredged when a famine forced them to and the pashas dredged when a shaykh paid them to, and in both cases the knowledge died with the engineer. What the register changes is small and total: a silted channel is now a line in a ledger with a date beside it, and somebody can be asked why the date has not moved.

options.text: Let the inspectors ride, and let them ride again next year.

destiny.name: The Gate of Hulwan
destiny.text: The Khurasan road leaves the Sawad at Hulwan, passes the rock at Behistun and does not level out until Hamadan, which the Greeks called Ecbatana. Every army that ever took Baghdad came down it, and so does half the water that feeds the eastern plain, because the Diyala and the Karkha both rise behind these ridges. Take Kermanshah and Hamadan and stand an army on the watershed: a state holding the plain and not the passes is holding a rich room with the door open.

conditions.text: Founding purpose: Dar al-Khilafa, the political capital.
Own Kermānšāh, or a subject owns it
Own Hamedān, or a subject owns it
Army size at least 30

event.title: The Gate of Hulwan
event.text:
The road climbs out of the Sawad at Hulwan and behind the first ridge it passes the rock at Behistun, where Darius had his account of a civil war carved too high up for anyone to reach and correct. It does not level out again until Hamadan. Every army that has ever come down onto this plain staged there first.

The caliphs learned this expensively, and so did the Buyids, who came out of these mountains themselves, and the Ilkhans, and everyone since. Two other things come down this way as well: the Diyala and the Karkha, which between them water the whole eastern half of the Sawad and rise behind the ridge we are now standing on. Baghdad is nine days from Hamadan for a courier and rather less than that for cavalry. The garrisons are placed now, the passes are held to the watershed, and for the first time in a long while the plain is being defended somewhere other than on the plain.

options.text: The door is shut and barred, and the bar is watched.

destiny.name: The Western Wing
destiny.text: Aleppo and Damascus were the other half of the caliphate and the only road to the sea that runs through nobody else's strait. Take them both, and hold half of the Levant around them, because Syria costs more to keep than to win.

conditions.text: Own Aleppo, or a subject owns it
Own Damascus, or a subject owns it
We or our subjects hold at least half of the locations in the Levant

event.title: The Western Wing
event.text:
Aleppo has given up its citadel and the Umayyad mosque at Damascus has heard the khutba read in Baghdad's name for the first time in six hundred years. The western half of the old caliphate is in hand, and with it the roads to the sea and the pilgrim route running south.

How to keep it is an older question, and Syria has only ever been answered two ways. The Umayyads cut the country into ajnad, military districts, each with a garrison paid from its own revenue under a governor deliberately sent from somewhere else. The Abbasids in their weakness did the opposite: they left the emirs of Aleppo, Hama and Damascus in their citadels and sent them robes of honour, a diploma and a title, and were obeyed for exactly as long as the robes kept arriving.

options.text: Cut it into ajnad. Iraqi garrisons, governors from outside.

modifiers.name: The Jund of Syria
modifiers.text: Syria cut into military districts on the Umayyad plan, each garrisoned out of Iraq under a governor from somewhere else. It holds, and the estates at home are paying for a great deal of marching they will never see.

options.text: Send robes of honour. The emirs keep their citadels.

modifiers.name: Investiture of the Emirs
modifiers.text: The lords of Aleppo, Hama and Damascus keep their citadels and hold them in Baghdad's name, on a robe of honour and a sealed diploma. Cheap, durable, and exactly as reliable as the next embassy.

destiny.name: The Shadow Caliph
destiny.text: An Abbasid has lived in Cairo on a Mamluk stipend since 1261, riding in processions and signing the diplomas that make sultans legitimate. Take Cairo and Jerusalem, keep an army and a name large enough to be believed, and bring the line home.

conditions.text: Own Cairo, or a subject owns it
Own Jerusalem, or a subject owns it
Prestige at least 75
Army size at least 75

event.title: The Shadow Caliph
event.text:
There has been an Abbasid in Cairo since 1261, when a survivor of the family reached Egypt and Baybars had him proclaimed within the month. His descendants have lived there ever since on a stipend, riding in processions, sealing the diplomas that make a Mamluk sultan lawful, and being kept away from any decision more consequential than the choice of a robe.

The household is ours now, and the city that kept it with them. What is done next settles what this state has been claiming all along. The banners can come out of storage and the claim can be made at full voice, which will be heard from Fez to Samarkand and answered by most of it. Or the man can be escorted home quietly and seated above a chancery, on the understanding that the writ which actually governs is the one with a seal at the bottom.

options.text: Raise the black. Let the khutba be read for Baghdad.

modifiers.name: The Black Banners
modifiers.text: The Abbasid black is out of storage and the khutba is read for Baghdad from Fez to Samarkand. Armies that march under it know what they are for, which is worth more than most things a treasury can buy.

options.text: Bring him home to a desk. Govern through the diwans.

modifiers.name: The Writ of the Diwans
modifiers.text: The caliph is seated above a chancery and the claim is exercised in seals, registers and the couriers who carry them. An establishment that large learns to skim before it learns anything else.

destiny.name: The Instruments of Maragha
destiny.text: Tusi's observatory on the hill above Maragha, paid for out of endowment revenue and staffed by men from Damascus, Mosul, Tiflis and China who could not always talk to each other except in numbers. Take Maragha, grow it into a town with a library worthy of the observatory, and build it up, because instruments are worth nothing without the men who read them.

conditions.text: Founding purpose: Madinat al-Salam, the civilizational capital.
Own Marāgheh, or a subject owns it
Maragheh is ours and has a library
Maragheh is ours and its development is at least 20

event.title: The Instruments of Maragha
event.text:
Hulagu let Tusi build it on the hill above the town and funded it out of endowment revenue, which is the only reason it outlived the man who paid for it. There is a quadrant cut into the rock on the meridian, an armillary sphere, a library nobody has ever counted honestly, and a staff that has included a Chinese astronomer alongside men from Damascus, Mosul and Tiflis who could not reliably talk to one another except in numbers.

The instruments are crated and roped and coming down the road, and rather more than half the staff has agreed to travel with them. What arrives is not a building. It is a method: observe for thirty years, write down everything including the failures, and never trust a table you have not checked against the sky yourself.

options.text: Unload them carefully. Find the men houses and pay them.

destiny.name: The Ingenious Devices
destiny.text: The Banu Musa's hundred machines, al-Jazari's crank that turns a wheel's circle into a pump's straight push, and the Sasanian weirs at Shushtar that have been lifting the Karun for a thousand years. Take Shushtar, raise head-works on three canals and have the silver ready, because the machinery is paid for before it earns.

conditions.text: Own Shūshtar, or a subject owns it
Canal Head-Works stand in at least 3 of our locations
Gold at least 2000

event.title: The Ingenious Devices
event.text:
Two books and one river settle this. The Banu Musa wrote the first in Baghdad, a hundred devices of valves and floats and lamps that trim themselves. Al-Jazari wrote the second at Amid and drew the crank that turns a wheel's circle into a pump's straight push, which is the single most useful drawing anyone in this country has made. Both books were received at court as amusements. Both describe machinery that lifts water.

The river is the Karun at Shushtar, where Shapur set captured Roman engineers to throw a weir across the stream with a bridge along the top of it, and cut a channel through solid rock to carry the overflow to the mills. It has been working for a thousand years. Our own engineers have measured it and come back quiet.

options.text: Put the machines on the land. Lift water to the terraces.

modifiers.name: The Water Engines
modifiers.text: Norias on the Euphrates terraces, dulabs on the Diyala, pumps where the bank is too high for either. Ground nobody would have ploughed is under crop, and the yards that built the machinery were paid long before it earned.

options.text: Keep them in the workshops. Clocks and quadrants sell.

modifiers.name: Clock and Quadrant
modifiers.text: Water clocks, astrolabes, graduated quadrants and lifting gear built to order in the Baghdad workshops and sold east and west. The market for a marvel has always been better than the market for a ditch.

destiny.name: The Corrected Tables
destiny.text: Samarkand holds the paper mills that came west after Talas and Ulugh Beg's sextant, sunk in a trench forty metres long. Take it, build Baghdad up around the Mustansiriya, and recompute the star catalogue for Baghdad's own meridian, because a zij is written for one latitude and is politely wrong everywhere else.

conditions.text: Own Samarkand, or a subject owns it
Gold at least 3000
Baghdad is ours, its development is at least 36 and the Mustansiriya stands there

event.title: The Corrected Tables
event.text:
Samarkand held two things Baghdad has always needed. The first is the mills that beat linen rag to pulp, the craft that came west after Talas and made a stationers' market possible here at all. The second is Ulugh Beg's sextant, sunk in a trench forty metres long, and the catalogue of a thousand and eighteen stars his people computed with it, the first in eight centuries that owed Ptolemy nothing.

The tables are being recomputed for the meridian of Baghdad, because a zij is written for one latitude and is politely wrong everywhere else. What the recomputation is for is the argument in the diwan now. The astronomers want the tax year fixed to the sun, since the lunar year runs a month ahead of the harvest every three decades and the kharaj keeps falling due before there is a crop to pay it with. The stationers want the eastern road kept open and the paper cheap.

options.text: Fix the kharaj year to the sun. Tax the crop, not the calendar.

modifiers.name: The Corrected Calendar
modifiers.text: The kharaj year is fixed to the sun, so the tax falls when the crop is in instead of drifting a month ahead of it every three decades. The jurists have views about calendars and none of them are quiet.

options.text: Keep the paper road open. Let a book cost what bread costs.

modifiers.name: The Road of Paper
modifiers.text: The Samarkand road is kept open and the mills are copied at home. A book stops being a bequest and becomes a commodity, which delights everyone except the men whose authority rested on owning one.

units.name: Madan Marshmen
units.text: Reed-skiff skirmishers of the Bataih who fight from the mashhuf and along causeways only they can find. On open flatland they are unarmoured men with fish spears.

units.name: Ayyarun
units.text: The sworn brotherhoods of the city quarters. Ferocious behind a barricade and worthless in a field formation: they break enemy morale and cannot take a charge.

units.name: Muntafiq Horse
units.text: Riders of the desert edge who choose whether a battle happens at all, and lose it when the enemy gets to choose instead.

units.name: Ghurab
units.text: The raven: a shallow oared gun-vessel that trades hull for guns. That is the right trade in a river mouth and the wrong one in open sea.

units.name: Kul Horsemen
units.text: The Georgian household of the Baghdad pashas, bought as boys and trained for a decade. There are never many and they take years to make, which is exactly why they ended up ruling Iraq.

buildings.name: Canal Head-Works
buildings.text: Masonry regulators at the offtake, so an engineer can decide how much river enters the canal and shut it when the flood comes down. Buildable only where there is a river or lake to tap.

buildings.name: Kharaj Diwan
buildings.text: The register office of the irrigated land: surveyors' ropes, tax rolls and the clerks who keep them. It knows what every jarib of the district owes and what it has paid.

buildings.name: Date Palm Grove
buildings.text: Palms planted in ranks along the riverbank among the fruit gardens of the arid river country, raised from offshoots of proven mothers and worked by climbers with rope and knife at pollination and again at harvest. The land's fruit harvest grows with them. Basra shipped its dates as far as China.

where.text: The location's raw material is Fruit

buildings.name: Suq al-Warraqin
buildings.text: The stationers' market: copyists working to order in the shopfronts, booksellers, and the readers who treat a bookseller's stock as a lending library. Over a hundred shops stood in the Baghdad original.

buildings.name: Al-Madrasa al-Mustansiriyya
buildings.text: Four iwans off one courtyard for the four schools of law, with a library, a hospital and a pharmacy behind them. It can only be built at Baghdad, because there is only one of it.

buildings.name: Shrine Precinct
buildings.text: The walled hadra of a great tomb, with its lodging, kitchens, burial ground and keeper families. Buildable only at the shrine cities themselves: Kufa, Karbala, Baghdad and Samarra.

buildings.name: Mudhif Redoubt
buildings.text: A reed hall on a made island, with the causeways and skiff channels that serve it. Buildable only in wetlands, which in Iraq means the Bataih and nowhere else.

buildings.name: Ubulla Wharf
buildings.text: The transhipment quay at the head of the Gulf, where sea-going hulls hand their cargo to river boats that can take the shoals upstream, and where the yards build both.

buildings.name: The Attabiya Looms
buildings.text: Master weavers laying a silk stripe on a cotton ground. Buildable only where the market carries cotton, which is the whole point of the attabi recipe.

where.text: Cotton is produced in the location's market

buildings.name: Qir Pits
buildings.text: Bitumen wells up from the ground at Hit and at al-Qayyara. It is skimmed off, boiled down and cut with sand into the mastic that keeps a hull tight.

buildings.name: Vilayet Press
buildings.text: The government press of a provincial seat. Baghdad had the first in 1869, and the gazette, the yearbooks and the schoolbooks of the province are printed there.

buildings.name: Dar al-Barid
buildings.text: A station of the caliphal post: stabling and remounts, a courier's room, sealed dispatch bags, and the sahib al-barid who lives here and whose real commission is to report on the governor next door. Buildable in the towns and cities of the old caliphal road network.

buildings.name: The Dulab Works
buildings.text: A yard that builds and repairs water-lifting machinery: the ox-driven dulab, the current-driven naura with its earthenware pots lashed to the rim, and the crank-and-piston pumps out of al-Jazari. Buildable on river and lake ground, because a machine that lifts water needs water under it.

buildings.name: The Marsad
buildings.text: An observatory: a quadrant cut on the meridian, a shop that files its own graduated brass, and a room of tables kept for the thirty years an observation programme actually takes. Cities only, and only under the sky its tables are written for.

list.name: Mirab and the Water Turn
list.text: The nawba is the turn: a measured span in which one village, and inside it one family, may draw from the canal. The mirab is the watermaster who keeps the turn list, opens and shuts the offtake, and calls out the yearly clearance that stops silt from closing the intake. Harun al-Rashid had the mouths of the Nahrawan shut, dug clean and reopened on that same principle between 786 and 806. Water in Mesopotamia is a ledger entry before it is a resource, and somebody has to keep the ledger.

list.name: Soyurghal
list.text: Soyurghal is the Mongol term for a grant made in perpetuity, and it is what the Jalayirids left behind them in Iraq. Qara Yusuf paid his emirs and his kinsmen out of the revenue of assigned land rather than in coin, and within a generation the assignment had hardened into a hereditary holding with its own immunity from tax. Uzun Hasan spent a reign trying to pull that revenue back into direct collection and never finished the work. An army that costs the treasury nothing is an army the treasury cannot recall.

list.name: The Jahbadhiyya
list.text: From 908 to 932 the wazirs of Baghdad kept two Jewish bankers on standing retainer, Yusuf ibn Finhas and Harun ibn Imran. They advanced the treasury a fixed sum on the first of every month against the revenue of Ahvaz, held the deposits of the merchant houses, and settled between Baghdad and the provinces on written order, the sakk that gave English its cheque. Ibn al-Furat could not govern without them and could not entirely trust them, which is the standing condition of any state that borrows.

conditions.text: Owns Baghdad

list.name: Naqib al-Ashraf
list.text: The naqib keeps the shajara, the register of those descended from the Prophet, entering their births and their deaths, judging their quarrels, paying their stipends and striking out the false claimants. Baghdad's niqaba was held around the year 1000 by Abu Ahmad al-Husayn ibn Musa, father of the poet al-Sharif al-Radi, and the office ran on under the Ottomans in the hands of the Gaylani house. In Iraq the register crosses the sectarian line instead of following it, because sayyid families and tribal shaykhs claim the same descent on both sides of it.
